title: Caching in System Design: A Handwritten Handbook
summary: A dense study-notes series on caching for system design: what caches are and why they work, the read/write patterns (cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back, write-around), TTL and expiry mechanics, eviction policies and their internals, invalidation strategies and consistency, distributed caching and hot keys, plus failure modes like stampedes, penetration, and stale reads.

chapters.title: Why Cache Exists: Locality and the Latency Gap
points: Definition: cache = small, fast store holding a copy of data whose authoritative home is a slower backing store (DB, disk, remote service, computed result).
Latency numbers to memorize: L1 ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD random read ~100µs, network RTT same-DC ~0.5ms, cross-region ~50-150ms, disk seek ~10ms. Cache buys 10x-1000x.
Caching only works because of locality: temporal (a key read now is likely read again soon) and spatial (nearby keys read together).
Access distributions are skewed, not uniform — Zipf's law: request rate of the rank-k item ∝ 1/k^s. Top 1% of keys can serve 50%+ of traffic, so a tiny cache gets a large hit rate.
Core metric: hit rate h. Average latency = h·T_cache + (1-h)·(T_cache + T_backend). Going 90%→95% hit rate halves backend load, not just 5% better.
Amdahl framing: cache only helps the fraction of time actually spent on the cached work. Caching a 5ms DB call inside a 500ms request is noise.
Two distinct goals: reduce latency (user-facing) and reduce load/cost (protect the origin). A cache can succeed at one and fail at the other.

Cache layers in a real system, client → origin: browser cache, CDN/edge, reverse proxy (Varnish/nginx), application in-process cache, distributed cache (Redis/Memcached), DB buffer pool, OS page cache, disk controller cache.
Working set = set of keys actively used in a time window. Cache smaller than working set → thrash; cache larger → wasted memory.
Every cache is a bet that data is read more often than it changes: read/write ratio is the single best screening signal for whether to cache at all.
Anti-case: caching is wrong for write-heavy, always-unique, or strict-freshness data (bank balance at time of transfer, one-time tokens, unique search queries).
Vocabulary set up front: hit, miss, eviction, expiration, invalidation, staleness, coherence, warm vs cold cache.

chapters.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
points: Pattern: application owns cache logic. Read: GET key from cache; on hit return; on miss read DB, SET key with TTL, return.

Canonical code:
v = cache.get(k)
if v is None:
    v = db.query(k)
    cache.set(k, v, ttl=300)
return v
Write path in cache-aside is usually write + delete (invalidate), not write + update: db.write(k,v); cache.delete(k).
Why delete beats update on write: updating writes a value that may never be read (wasted work) and reintroduces the lost-update race between concurrent writers.
Advantages: only requested data is cached (memory follows real demand); cache node failure is survivable — misses fall through to DB; cache and DB models can differ (cache a joined DTO, not a row).
Disadvantages: every first read is a miss → 3 trips on cold path; cold start after a flush hammers the DB; consistency is the app's responsibility, duplicated at every call site.

Classic race — stale set: reader misses, reads DB v1, stalls; writer commits v2 and deletes key; reader then SETs v1. Cache now holds v1 until TTL. Fixes: short TTL, versioned keys, delete-after-delay (dual delete), or CAS/set-if-not-exists.
Mitigation for cold-start misses: prewarm/seed the cache on deploy for known-hot keys, and stagger TTLs so a batch loaded together doesn't expire together.
Read-through contrast: same read semantics, but the cache library/provider does the DB load on miss, so the app just calls get(). Cache-aside = app-managed; read-through = cache-managed loader.
Read-through requires the cache to know how to fetch (a loader function, e.g. Caffeine LoadingCache / Guava CacheLoader) and forces the cache model to mirror the DB model.
Cache-aside is the default choice for most web systems: simplest to reason about, degrades gracefully, works with any store.
Gotcha: cache the miss too. If a key legitimately doesn't exist, store a null/tombstone with a short TTL or the miss path is repeated on every request (see cache penetration).

chapters.title: Write Patterns: Write-Through, Write-Back, Write-Around
points: Write-through: app writes to cache, cache synchronously writes to DB, then acknowledges. Cache is always consistent with DB for cached keys.
Write-through cost: every write pays cache + DB latency; writes to keys never read waste cache space. Pair with a TTL to evict cold written keys.
Write-back (write-behind): write lands in cache and is acknowledged immediately; the DB is updated asynchronously, often batched/coalesced.
Write-back wins: lowest write latency, absorbs write bursts, coalesces repeated writes to the same key into one DB write (huge for counters, view counts, last-seen timestamps).
Write-back risk: data loss window if a cache node dies with dirty entries unflushed. Needs replication, an append-only log/WAL, or acceptance that the data is not durable.
Dirty bit: write-back caches mark entries dirty; eviction of a dirty entry must flush to the backing store first, so eviction becomes a write path.
Write-around: writes go straight to DB, bypassing the cache (and typically invalidating the key). Good for write-heavy data that is rarely re-read.
Write-around downside: a key just written is a guaranteed miss on the next read — bad for read-your-own-writes.
Combination in practice: cache-aside reads + write-around/invalidate writes is the most common real-world pairing; write-through + read-through is the most common in-library/embedded pairing.

Comparison table — Pattern | Write latency | Read-after-write | Durability risk | Best for: Write-through | high | fresh | none | read-heavy, needs freshness. Write-back | lowest | fresh | data loss | write-heavy, tolerant. Write-around | DB latency | miss (stale risk) | none | write-heavy, rarely read. Cache-aside+delete | DB latency | miss then fresh | none | general purpose.
Ordering rule for cache-aside writes: write DB first, then invalidate cache. Invalidating first leaves a window where a concurrent read repopulates the old value before the DB commit.
Double-delete (delayed dual invalidation): delete cache → write DB → sleep ~a few hundred ms → delete cache again, to kill any stale value a concurrent reader wrote in between.

chapters.title: TTL and Expiration Mechanics
points: TTL = time-to-live: max age after which an entry is treated as invalid. It's the safety net that bounds staleness even when invalidation logic is buggy or misses an event.
Absolute expiry (expire at fixed instant) vs sliding expiry (each access extends the deadline). Sliding keeps hot keys alive; risk is a key that never expires and never refreshes.
TTL choice = staleness budget: 'how out-of-date may this be before a user notices or a rule breaks?' Session data seconds-minutes, product catalog minutes-hours, country list days.

Expiration enforcement strategies: lazy/passive (check on read, expire then), active/scheduled sampling (background job samples and reaps), and eviction-on-pressure. Redis uses lazy + sampled active expiry, so expired keys can hold memory until reaped.
Expired ≠ evicted: expiration is time-driven and semantic; eviction is capacity-driven and opportunistic. Both remove entries but for unrelated reasons.
TTL jitter is mandatory at scale: set ttl = base + random(0, base·0.1..0.2). Without jitter, keys loaded together expire together and produce a synchronized miss storm.
Negative caching: give not-found results a short TTL (e.g. 30-60s) so repeated lookups for absent keys don't reach the DB.

Refresh-ahead / stale-while-revalidate: serve the stale value immediately and asynchronously refresh in the background — hides refresh latency, keeps hit rate high, at the cost of one extra staleness interval.
Two-TTL scheme: a 'soft' TTL (after which a background refresh is triggered but the value is still served) and a 'hard' TTL (after which the value must not be served).

HTTP mapping: Cache-Control: max-age=N is TTL; s-maxage targets shared caches; stale-while-revalidate=N and stale-if-error=N are the refresh-ahead and fail-open knobs; ETag/If-None-Match gives 304 revalidation without re-sending the body.
Set TTL at write time, not by scanning later; and never leave a cached key with no TTL unless it is explicitly invalidated — no-TTL keys are the main cause of unbounded cache growth.
Gotcha: TTL does not fix consistency, it only bounds the damage. A 5-minute TTL means up to 5 minutes of every user seeing a wrong value.

chapters.title: Eviction Policies and Their Internals
points: Eviction happens when the cache is full and a new entry needs space; the policy decides the victim. Goal: approximate Bélády's optimal (evict the item used furthest in the future), which is unimplementable, so all policies are heuristics.
LRU (least recently used): evict the entry untouched longest. Implementation: hash map + doubly linked list; on access, unlink node and move to head — O(1) get and put.
LRU weakness: scan resistance. One full table scan or batch job touches every key once and flushes the entire hot set.

LFU (least frequently used): evict the lowest access count. Better for stable skewed workloads; weakness is cache pollution — an old key with a huge count never leaves. Fix with count aging/decay (halve counters periodically) or a windowed count.
Redis approximates both: allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu sample N random keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) rather than maintaining a true global list — near-LRU quality at far lower cost.
LFU in Redis uses an 8-bit logarithmic counter (probabilistic increment) plus a decay time, so frequency fits in the existing object metadata.

FIFO: evict the oldest inserted regardless of use. Cheap, poor hit rate. CLOCK/Second-chance: FIFO ring with a reference bit — approximates LRU without a per-access list update; used in OS page replacement.
Segmented / SLRU and ARC: split into probationary and protected segments so a one-hit key can't evict a long-lived hot key; ARC self-tunes the split between recency and frequency.

W-TinyLFU (Caffeine's default): a small LRU admission window in front of a frequency sketch (Count-Min Sketch); a new key is only admitted if its estimated frequency beats the victim's. Near-optimal hit rates at tiny metadata cost.
Random / allkeys-random: no bookkeeping; surprisingly acceptable at very high hit rates and used as a fallback under pressure.

TTL-aware policies: Redis volatile-lru / volatile-lfu / volatile-ttl / volatile-random consider only keys that have a TTL set — so keys without a TTL are never evicted, and a full cache of TTL-less keys returns OOM errors on write.
noeviction policy: reject writes with an error when full. Correct choice when the store is used as a queue or source of truth, dangerous when used as a cache.

Comparison row set — Policy | Bookkeeping cost | Scan-resistant? | Best workload: LRU | O(1) list ops | no | recency-driven. LFU | counters + aging | yes | stable skew. FIFO | trivial | no | uniform. CLOCK | 1 bit/entry | partly | OS paging. W-TinyLFU | sketch | yes | mixed real traffic.
Measure, don't assume: track evictions/sec, hit rate, and memory fragmentation together. Rising evictions with falling hit rate = cache is undersized for the working set.

chapters.title: Invalidation: Keeping the Copy Honest
points: Invalidation = removing/updating a cached copy because the truth changed. Distinct from expiration (time) and eviction (space).
Three mechanisms: explicit delete on write, TTL-only (accept bounded staleness), and event/CDC-driven (subscribe to the DB change stream — Debezium, binlog, outbox — and invalidate).

Key design determines invalidation difficulty. Flat, deterministic keys (user:123:profile) are easy; derived/aggregate keys (feed:123, leaderboard:top10) are hard because a single write invalidates many keys.
Versioned keys (key stamping): include a version or updated_at in the key — user:123:v7. A write bumps the version; old entries become unreferenced and die by eviction/TTL. No delete needed, no race.

Namespace/generation invalidation: store a generation counter (products:gen = 42) and prefix keys with it. Bumping the generation invalidates a whole family in one write — the standard 'group flush' trick.
Tag-based invalidation: attach tags to entries and invalidate by tag (used by CDNs — Fastly surrogate keys, Varnish bans). Cost is maintaining the tag→key index.

Cache coherence in a multi-node in-process cache: each app node has its own copy, so a delete must be broadcast (pub/sub, Redis keyspace notifications, gossip). Without a broadcast, nodes drift independently.
Read-your-own-writes: after a user's own write, either invalidate synchronously before responding, or pin that user to read from primary/skip cache for a short window.
Ordering hazards: DB write and cache delete are not atomic. If the process dies between them the cache is stale until TTL — which is exactly why every key still needs a TTL.
Transactional outbox/CDC gives at-least-once invalidation with correct ordering, at the cost of pipeline lag (typically hundreds of ms).
Invalidating too broadly (flush all) trades correctness for a thundering herd on the origin. Prefer targeted or generation-based invalidation.
Rule of thumb hierarchy, safest to riskiest: versioned keys > CDC-driven delete > write-then-delete > write-then-update > TTL only.

chapters.title: Distributed Caching: Placement, Sharding, Hot Keys
points: Local (in-process) cache: nanosecond access, no network, but per-node duplication, no coherence, and lost on restart. Examples: Caffeine, Guava, Ehcache.
Remote/shared cache: one logical copy, coherent across nodes, survives app restarts, but costs a network round-trip and serialization. Examples: Redis, Memcached.
Near-cache / two-tier (L1 local + L2 remote): best latency with bounded duplication; needs invalidation broadcast to keep L1 honest. This is where most stale-data bugs live.
Sharding by consistent hashing: keys map to points on a hash ring so adding/removing a node remaps only ~1/N of keys, not all of them (as modulo hashing would).
Virtual nodes (replicas per physical node on the ring) smooth load imbalance and make node removal spread evenly.
Rendezvous (HRW) hashing as an alternative: pick the node maximizing hash(key,node) — no ring, same minimal-disruption property.

Hot key problem: one viral key concentrates all traffic on one shard. Fixes: replicate the key across N shards with a random suffix (key:hot:{0..9}), promote it to a local L1 cache on every app node, or front it with a request-coalescing layer.
Hot shard vs hot key: uneven key-space distribution vs a single dominant key — diagnose before fixing, the remedies differ.

Memcached vs Redis: Memcached is multithreaded, strings only, pure LRU cache, trivially scalable; Redis is (mostly) single-threaded per shard with rich types, persistence, replication, Lua, pub/sub, and Cluster. Choose Memcached for a pure large-object cache, Redis when you need structures or durability.
Serialization matters: JSON is debuggable but slow and large; protobuf/msgpack cut CPU and memory significantly on hot paths. Cost of serialization can exceed the DB call for small values.
Connection handling: use pooling and pipelining; a Redis round-trip is fast, but 50 sequential GETs in one request is 50 RTTs — batch with MGET or a pipeline.
Client-side vs proxy-based topology: client-side hashing (Memcached, Redis Cluster clients) is fastest; a proxy (Envoy, twemproxy, mcrouter) centralizes routing and failover at the cost of a hop.

chapters.title: Failure Modes: Stampede, Penetration, Avalanche, Staleness
points: Cache stampede (thundering herd / dogpile): a hot key expires and N concurrent requests all miss and hit the DB simultaneously. Load spike is proportional to concurrency, not to traffic growth.

Stampede fix 1 — mutex/single-flight: the first misser takes a lock (SET NX with a short TTL) and recomputes; others wait briefly or serve the stale value. Go's singleflight, Java's LoadingCache do this per key.
Stampede fix 2 — probabilistic early expiration (XFetch): refresh early with probability rising as the TTL approaches, so one request refreshes before the cliff instead of all at once.
Stampede fix 3 — never expire hot keys: keep a logical expiry inside the value, always serve it, and trigger an async refresh when logically stale.

Cache penetration: requests for keys that don't exist in the DB either (scrapers, enumeration attacks) always miss and always reach the DB. Fix: negative caching with short TTL, plus a Bloom filter of existing IDs to reject unknowns in O(1).
Bloom filter trade-off: no false negatives, tunable false positives — a false positive only costs one wasted DB lookup, which is exactly the acceptable error direction.

Cache avalanche: a large set of keys expires at once (same TTL from a bulk load) or the cache cluster restarts cold; the origin receives full traffic and collapses. Fixes: TTL jitter, staged warmup, request rate limiting/load shedding at the origin, circuit breakers.
Cold start after failover is the same failure with a different trigger — a cache that a system cannot survive without is not a cache, it's an undeclared dependency. Capacity-plan for hit rate = 0.

Stale reads from replication lag: write to primary, invalidate cache, then a read repopulates the cache from a lagging read replica — cache now holds pre-write data. Fix by reading from primary during the invalidation window or delaying the second delete beyond replica lag.
Metrics that reveal these: hit rate, miss rate, evictions/sec, expired keys/sec, p99 get latency, origin QPS, and lock-wait counts. Alert on origin QPS spikes, not just cache metrics.
Big-value trap: caching multi-MB blobs in Redis blocks the event loop on serialization and network write, hurting every other key. Split, compress, or push large blobs to object storage + CDN.

Security note: caches keyed on user-controlled input can leak data across users if the key omits the tenant/user dimension — the classic 'cached the wrong user's page' bug. Always include the full authorization context in the key.

chapters.title: Design Checklist and Cheatsheet
points: Screening questions before adding a cache: What's the read/write ratio? What's the staleness budget? What's the working-set size? What breaks if the cache is empty? What breaks if it serves a stale value?
Sizing: memory ≈ working_set_keys × (key + value + overhead). Redis per-key overhead is ~50-100 bytes, so millions of tiny keys are dominated by metadata — batch into hashes if so.
Target hit rate depends on the goal: to cut latency, care about p99 hits; to protect the origin, compute the surviving origin QPS = total_QPS × (1 - h) and make sure the origin can serve it.
Key naming convention: entity:id:field:version, plus a tenant/user dimension whenever the data is scoped. Consistent naming makes generation-based flushes possible later.
Default recipe for a read-heavy web service: cache-aside reads + write-then-delete invalidation + TTL with jitter + negative caching + single-flight on miss + allkeys-lru eviction.
Pattern decision table — need lowest write latency → write-back; need cache always correct on write → write-through; writes rarely re-read → write-around; anything else → cache-aside.
Eviction decision table — recency-driven traffic → LRU; stable popularity skew → LFU/TinyLFU; must never evict, only expire → noeviction + strict TTLs; mixed real traffic → W-TinyLFU.

Invalidation decision table — can tolerate minutes of staleness → TTL only; must be prompt and keys are simple → write-then-delete; derived/fan-out keys → generation counters or tags; must be correct across regions → CDC/event-driven.

Common mistakes recap: no TTL on any key; identical TTLs (avalanche); invalidating before the DB commit; caching per-user data under a shared key; caching the failure of a downstream call forever; treating the cache as durable storage; measuring hit rate but not origin QPS.

Testing a cache: run with the cache disabled (does the system still work?), run cold (does it survive?), run with a forced flush under load (does it stampede?), and assert staleness bounds in integration tests.
Observability minimum: hit/miss counters per key-prefix, eviction and expiry rates, memory used vs maxmemory, and a dashboard panel for origin QPS overlaid with cache hit rate.

One-line summary of the whole handbook: a cache is a bounded, expiring, evictable copy — TTL bounds how wrong it can be, eviction bounds how big it can get, invalidation bounds how long it stays wrong, and every pattern choice is just where you put the write.
